feedback: If the crumple model doesn't raise a ridge, push more slowly and firmly so the sheets buckle upward rather than slide flat.
If a learner can't explain the subduction volcano, trace the chain aloud: plate dives → heats up and releases water → rock above it partly melts → magma rises → volcano.
Ask the learner to match each physical model to a real place and its hazard signature.
activities.intendedInsight: The abstract motions become physical actions, and the collision→mountains and subduction→volcano links become something the learner has built with their hands before naming.
learnerActions: Enact pushing together, pulling apart, and sliding past using foam blocks, your two hands, or biscuits/graham crackers resting on a soft filling (e.g. frosting).
Crumple two sheets of paper or two rugs by pushing them together to raise a ridge — model how collision crumples crust into mountains.

For subduction, push two blocks together and let one slide under the other; describe how the diving plate heats up and releases water, which makes the hot rock above it partly melt, feeding magma that rises to a volcano.
Name each motion only after you have physically done it, then predict what hazard or landform it would create.
activities.title: Hands-on plate models with everyday materials

feedback: Correct answer to the diagnostic: the friend is wrong — what happens depends on how the plates move. Push together (convergent) → mountains, and a plate can dive under, releasing water so that rock above it partly melts to feed volcanoes; pull apart (divergent) → magma rises to make new crust and volcanoes; slide past (transform) → mainly earthquakes, usually no volcanoes. Earthquakes can happen at all three, but the type of movement controls the landforms and whether volcanoes form.
If a learner gives one generic result for every boundary, place push/pull/slide outcomes side by side (mountains / new crust / earthquakes).
If a learner treats earthquakes/volcanoes as unrelated to plate movement, stress that the grinding, colliding and spreading AT boundaries is exactly what triggers them.
If a learner thinks collision mountains appear quickly or in one event, note that uplift is slow, happening over millions of years of continued pushing.

Probe deeper: What rises to fill the gap where plates pull apart, and what does it build? Why big earthquakes but usually no volcanoes where plates slide past? What forms when two plates push straight into each other? How long does a mountain range take to rise at a collision boundary?
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and correct application of the motion→feature rules, and explicit rejection of the 'same everywhere' idea by explaining what differs by motion type.
learnerActions: Match each boundary type to its hazard/landform.
Categorize real places by boundary type: sort Himalayas (collision), Iceland/Mid-Atlantic Ridge (spreading), San Andreas (sliding).
Sequence a subduction chain in order: plate dives → heats up and releases water → rock above it partly melts → magma rises → volcano erupts.

Answer the diagnostic: 'At one place two plates push together; at another they slide past. A friend says it doesn't matter how plates meet — you get the same thing everywhere. Do you agree? What differs depending on HOW they meet?'
activities.title: Consolidate and sort: match, categorize, sequence

feedback: Ask the learner to point to where the diving plate releases water and the rock above it partly melts, and where magma rises, as they rotate the model.
Prompt: which view (3D block or 2D slice) helped you see the subduction depth, and which helped you read the labels?
activities.intendedInsight: Subduction and collision happen in three dimensions; a depth view can make the diving plate easier to picture, complementing the cross-section view.
learnerActions: If available, manipulate a 3D plate-block model you can push, pull, and slide, and rotate to view from any angle.
Look along the depth of the model to see a subducting plate diving beneath another.
Compare the 3D depth view with the 2D cross-sections you used earlier and describe what each view shows more clearly.
activities.title: Extension: 3D block model of subduction and collision
